_doc: Measurement journal: one entry per patch, newest last. Values are read from the source files at build time (scripts/build_site.py); tests/test_journal.py checks every source.

overview.what: taintwall is a runtime for AI agents that hold a crypto wallet. It defends against prompt injection by design: the model that plans never reads untrusted data, every value carries a label saying where it came from, and policies check those labels before any tool runs.
overview.goal: Cut the attack success rate to near zero while keeping utility close to the undefended agent's.
overview.now: Stage 2 measures the planner itself, without policies: on AgentDojo banking it keeps most of the plain agent's utility; retries rescue failing programs but no scores. The strongest attack on the undefended agent is memory injection.

highlights.note: memory injection on CrAIBench crypto_trading, undefended agent: the attack taintwall must stop
prompt injection through tool output on AgentDojo banking: this model already refuses it
utility of the undefended agent on AgentDojo banking: what the defense may not lose
plans our plan language accepts when the planner is told the rules (Haiku 5.5)

glossary: Utility
Share of normal tasks the agent completes correctly. Higher is better.
ASR
Attack success rate: share of attacked tasks in which the attacker's goal was achieved. Lower is better; the target is 0%.
Utility under attack
Share of tasks still completed correctly while an attack is present.
Prompt injection
Attacker text hidden in data a tool returns (a file, a transaction subject, a web page).
Memory injection
Attacker text planted in the agent's memory, so it later reads as the agent's own past notes.
important_instructions, tool_knowledge
AgentDojo's attack templates: an urgent instruction addressed to the model, and one that also names the tools to call.
Plain agent
The benchmark's own tool-calling agent with no defense: the baseline taintwall is compared with.
Plans accepted
Share of plans written by a model that the taintwall plan language accepts as written.
95% CI
The range the true rate lies in with 95% confidence (Wilson interval). With 16 tasks it is wide.
pp
Percentage points: the difference between two percentages (60% to 70% is +10 pp).
Better, worse, within noise
A change counts as better or worse only when the two 95% intervals do not overlap; otherwise it is within noise.
Kinds
baseline: the undefended reference; study: a measurement that informs a design decision; change: a patch without a new measurement; defense: taintwall itself measured.

patches.title: Provenance labels and the explicit-flow interpreter
patches.changed: Labeled values with sources and readers; a plan interpreter for a checked Python subset that labels every value it computes; clean-code and mutation gates in CI.
patches.why: The core every later measurement depends on. No benchmark yet: the defense is not wired to a planner.

patches.title: Baseline: plain agent on AgentDojo banking
patches.changed: First benchmark run: AgentDojo's undefended tool-calling agent, Haiku 5.5 through OpenRouter, all 16 banking tasks and 144 attack pairs.
patches.question: What does an agent without any defense score, so taintwall has something to beat?
patches.result: Utility 69%. The important_instructions attack never succeeds: Haiku 5.5 names the injected block and refuses it.
patches.decision: Prompt injection through tool output is not where this model fails; look for a stronger channel (tool_knowledge, memory).

patches.title: Baseline: tool_knowledge attack and CrAIBench
patches.changed: A stronger AgentDojo attack (tool_knowledge) and the CrAIBench crypto suites (chain, dao_nft, crypto_trading) with prompt and memory injection, same plain agent.
patches.question: Is there an attack channel that works on this model, for taintwall to close?
patches.result: Prompt injection stays at 0–4%. Memory injection succeeds in 48–67% of pairs: CrAIBench inserts the planted memory as a user message, so the model takes attacker text for the owner's words.
patches.decision: Memory injection is the main comparison for contribution B (labels that persist in memory).

patches.title: Implicit flows: if, for and while, strict and lenient
patches.changed: Control flow in plans with a pc label; strict mode puts the conditions a value depends on into its label; every run-time failure carries the label of what it depends on. Stage 1 complete.
patches.why: Without it a plan could leak a secret through which branch it takes. Still no planner, so no benchmark change.

patches.title: Study: what Python planners write
patches.changed: Five models wrote plans for the 16 banking tasks, without and with the plan language stated in the prompt. Nothing executed.
patches.question: How much of what planners write does the plan language accept, and what must it add?
patches.result: Stating the language is the main lever (Haiku 0% → 88%, GPT-5 mini 0% → 62%). DeepSeek V3.2 ignores most rules (19%). String methods, number formats and `is None` survive the rules for every model.
patches.decision: Add those constructs in PR 1; the planner prompt states the rules; per-model output budgets (a first run with 2000 tokens, $0.18 of the cost, was discarded: hidden reasoning cut 15 of 160 replies).

patches.title: Plan language v2: what planners keep writing
patches.changed: The plan language accepts string methods, `record.get`, fixed-point number formats, `x is None`, `a if c else b`, `x += y` and the builtins `round`, `int`, `float`, `str`, `bool`, `range`, `sorted`, `any`, `all`, each labeled by what its result depends on. The later operands of `and`/`or` and the branch of `a if c else b` now run under a pc of what decided them.
patches.question: With the constructs the study asked for, how many of the same plans does the language accept?
patches.result: The same 160 plans, recounted: with rules in the prompt Haiku 5.5 reaches 100%, DeepSeek V3.2 goes from 19% to 88% and GPT-5 mini from 62% to 94%; Llama 4 Scout stays at 44% (its plans define functions and use comprehensions). No model calls: the plans are those of the study.
patches.decision: Keep `def`, comprehensions, slices and imports out; the static checker and typed retry (PR 2, PR 4) turn what remains into fixable errors. Accepted is still not correct: that is measured in PR 5.

patches.title: Static plan checker
patches.changed: Before a plan runs, the checker reads it against the tool specs and reports every statement that would fail whatever the data: unknown tools, names read before anything binds them, arguments that do not fit a tool, builtin or method, fields a record type lacks, indexes, loops and f-string parts a value cannot take, a tool's name reused. Errors are typed codes from the plan text only; it also lists every call with its effects and its constant arguments, for one approval per plan.
patches.question: Of the plans the language accepts, how many does the checker still stop, and are those real mistakes?
patches.result: 21 of the 91 accepted plans of the study (natural and rules runs together) have a statement that cannot succeed. 16 format a record or a tuple in an f-string, most often the dict `send_money` returns (`f"... Result: {result}"`); 3 call `str()` on a list of transactions to hand it to the reader; one loops over a string and one passes a reader schema as a list (refused against the reader as the study prompt states it). A straight-line plan that runs is never refused (property tests on generated plans).
patches.decision: Ship the checker as the first loop of the typed retry (PR 4): its errors are safe to show and cover one plan in four here. The planner prompt should say that only atoms can be formatted or converted with `str()`, and that the reader takes records and tuples as they are. What the plans get wrong at run time, with data, is what PR 5 measures.

patches.title: The planner on AgentDojo banking, with retries and one shot
patches.changed: AgentDojo's banking suite through taintwall's planner: the P-LLM writes a program without seeing data, the checker and the interpreter run it, the reader extracts fields from what it reads, and what it answers is scored. No policies yet. Two settings: Q3's retries, Replan(2, 1), and CaMeL's one shot, Replan(0, 0).
patches.question: What does the planner/reader split cost in utility, and how often do plans fail, with and without retries?
patches.result: Utility 56% with retries and one shot alike, against 69% for the plain agent (intervals overlap on 16 tasks). On a shared cache, so paired, retries rescue 11 and 7 of 144 attacked requests (plan failure 28% to 22%, 29% to 25%) but change no score: the rescued task's check always passes. ASR is 0% as for the plain agent, which already refuses these attacks. The largest loss is the reader being all or nothing: a plan asking for one field the data lacks fails the whole call (3 of 16 tasks).
patches.decision: Let the reader return what it found (optional fields); keep Replan(2, 1) as the default with one shot measured on the same cache, and judge retries again on CrAIBench; state data conventions such as `"me"` in tool descriptions. Attacks are measured where the plain agent fails: memory injection on CrAIBench.
